clue.text: Mince pies first for old fighters

indicators.note: to mince is to chop finely, so the words that follow are cut up and rearranged

blocks.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Veteran warriors are first in the queue for Christmas mince pies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mince pies' reads as one festive item, but 'Mince' is the instruction and 'pies first' the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spitfire was the celebrated British fighter aircraft of the Second World War, now long retired from service.

clue.text: Employees held in the utmost affection

indicators.note: something held in another phrase sits inside it, so the letters lie within the next words

blocks.note: found running across the end of utmost and the start of affection

explanation.surface: A boss who holds the workforce in the highest regard.
explanation.definitionFit: Staff is the collective noun for the people employed by an organisation.

clue.text: Bliss, perhaps, composing nice organ pieces?

indicators.note: composing means putting together something new, so the letters are arranged afresh
something in pieces has been broken up, so the letters are free to be put back in another order

blocks.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Is writing pleasant organ music a kind of bliss?
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the proverb 'ignorance is bliss', so bliss is offered as a quality that ignorance may be.
explanation.definitionFit: The saying 'where ignorance is bliss, 'tis folly to be wise' pairs the two, so bliss may stand for not knowing.

clue.text: People heading for England put on weight in this port

indicators.note: a heading is what comes at the top, so only the opening letter of the next word is used

blocks.note: folk are people
the first letter of England
a stone is a British unit of weight, fourteen pounds

explanation.surface: Passengers bound for England gain a few pounds in this harbour town.
explanation.walkthrough: Folkestone is a Channel port in Kent; the stone is the British weight unit of fourteen pounds still used for body weight.
explanation.definitionFit: Folkestone is a harbour town on the Kent coast, long a ferry crossing point to France.

clue.text: Engineers, worn out, went to bed

blocks.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, a corps of the British Army
tired means exhausted

explanation.surface: Exhausted army engineers turned in for the night.
explanation.definitionFit: To retire can mean to go to bed for the night, as in 'retire for the evening'.

clue.text: Not much time for another helping

blocks.note: first meaning: a few brief moments
second meaning: a further portion of food at a meal

explanation.surface: No time to go back to the buffet for more food.
explanation.definitionFit: The plural noun means both brief units of time and a second serving of food taken after the first.

clue.text: Singular stuff? Beat it!

blocks.note: S is the grammatical abbreviation for singular
to cram is to stuff full

explanation.surface: Someone told off for odd stuff and ordered to leave.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal commands telling someone to go away at once.

clue.text: Leave out refuse container

blocks.note: first meaning: to omit or pass over
second meaning: in Britain, a large open bin for builders' rubbish

explanation.surface: Put the rubbish bin outside.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a skip is a large open metal bin hired for building waste.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a verb for omitting something and a British noun for a big rubbish container.

clue.text: Acknowledgement that may be jolly?

definitions.note: a descriptive clause rather than a noun

blocks.note: first meaning: radio slang for 'message received'
second meaning: the pirate flag is the Jolly ...

explanation.surface: A cheerful reply confirming a message.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half points to the Jolly Roger, the skull-and-crossbones pirate flag.
explanation.definitionFit: Radio operators say this word to confirm receipt, and it is also the name preceded by 'Jolly' for the pirate flag.

clue.text: Armaments ordered for soldiers

indicators.note: ordered here means put into a new arrangement, so the letters are sorted differently

blocks.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Weapons purchased to equip the troops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ordered' reads as 'purchased' in the surface but signals rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Men-at-arms is an old term for armed fighting men, especially medieval troops.

clue.text: Quash urban legend started by girl

indicators.note: what has only been started has just its opening letters in place, so only the first of each word counts

blocks.note: a common girl's name
the first letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A girl spreads an urban myth that someone wants stopped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By' means beside: the girl's name sits next to the initials.
explanation.definitionFit: To annul a ruling is to quash it, declaring it void in law.

clue.text: Adding nothing new after changing course

indicators.note: after places the short pieces behind the longer one in the finished word

blocks.note: a sailing boat tacks when it changes course against the wind
O is zero, nothing
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A sailor contributes nothing fresh after altering direction.
explanation.definitionFit: Tacking on means appending something extra to what is already there.

clue.text: In favour of supporting patient

blocks.note: for means in support of
bearing a load is supporting it

explanation.surface: A hospital patient who is backed and propped up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Patient' looks like a noun for a hospital case but is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Forbearing describes someone tolerant and slow to lose their temper, the adjective sense of patient.

clue.text: Guitarist puts his finger on this worry

definitions.text: Guitarist puts his finger on this

blocks.clueFragment: Guitarist puts his finger on this
blocks.note: first meaning: a raised ridge across a guitar's neck
second meaning: to be anxious

explanation.surface: A guitarist pins down exactly what is bothering them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Puts his finger on' sounds like identifying the cause of a worry, but is literal fingering.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names the metal ridges on a guitar fingerboard and also means to be anxious or agitated.

clue.text: Think again about drink old bridge partners brought in

indicators.note: what is brought in is taken inside, so these letters go within the drink

blocks.note: re means about or concerning
cider is an alcoholic drink made from apples
O is the abbreviation for old
North and South are partners at the bridge table

explanation.surface: A drinker reconsiders after old bridge partners are invited round.
explanation.walkthrough: The old letter and the bridge pair go together inside the drink, after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To reconsider is to think about something a second time, perhaps to change one's mind.

clue.text: Marked?  Indeed not!

indicators.note: the clue's opening In, split off from the rest, says one word sits inside another

blocks.note: read as two words, 'in deed'; the second word is the outer piece
taken as written

explanation.surface: A curt exchange: was it noted? Absolutely not!
explanation.walkthrough: The trick is to break 'Indeed' into two words, so 'In' becomes a container signal. It looks like an anagram, but there is no anagram indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: Denoted means indicated or signified, as a symbol marks or stands for something.

clue.text: Word for young Robin, say?

blocks.note: first meaning: rhyming slang
second meaning: a child's term for a small bird, a robin being an example

explanation.surface: A name used when talking to a little boy called Robin.
explanation.walkthrough: Dicky bird is Cockney rhyming slang for word; 'young' signals the nursery term for a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is both nursery talk for a little bird and rhyming slang for a single word.

clue.text: Football player beginning to sob? Crybaby!

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that is taken

blocks.note: the first letter of sob
a crybaby is one who weeps

explanation.surface: A footballer starts to blub and is mocked as a crybaby.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweeper is a football defender who plays behind the back line clearing loose balls.

clue.text: Stop protecting Capone — it's very common

indicators.note: to protect something is to surround and shield it, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: to prevent is to stop
Al Capone, the Chicago gangster

explanation.surface: Stop shielding the gangster Capone, since such crime is widespread.
explanation.definitionFit: Prevalent means widespread or existing commonly at a given time.

clue.text: Eels can swim to get clear of dirt

definitions.note: a verb phrase, matching the verb

indicators.note: things that swim move about freely, so the letters drift into a new order

blocks.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Eels go swimming to wash off the mud.
explanation.definitionFit: To cleanse is to make thoroughly clean, freeing something of dirt.

clue.text: Period of darkness expected at first after energy cuts

indicators.note: at first points to the opening of the word just before, so only its initial is used

blocks.note: E is the symbol for energy
clips means trims or cuts
the first letter of expected

explanation.surface: A blackout was predicted once the power supply was cut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' places the expected initial behind the other pieces; 'energy cuts' looks like a power outage but is two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: During an eclipse the sun's light is blocked, giving a spell of darkness.

clue.text: Pained expression covered by reporters showing skill

indicators.note: what is covered by something is wrapped inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: the press are journalists
ow is a cry of pain

explanation.surface: A grimace caught by the paparazzi reveals some talent.
explanation.definitionFit: Prowess is outstanding ability or expertise in a particular field.

clue.text: Obtain professional medical treatment

blocks.note: pro is short for professional
a cure is a remedy

explanation.surface: Get expert medical care.
explanation.definitionFit: To procure is to acquire or get hold of something, often with some effort.

clue.text: American tug

blocks.note: first meaning: informal term for someone from the USA
second meaning: a sharp pull

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests an American tugboat; the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is slang for a person from the United States and also a verb or noun for a sudden pull.

clue.text: Like a crab that's cold?

blocks.note: first meaning: inclined to pinch with its claws
second meaning: chilly

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a crab is feeling the chill.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means apt to pinch, as a crab does, and is informal for sharply chilly weather.

clue.text: Disturbed soil — not bad clue for Holmes, perhaps

indicators.note: something disturbed has been moved out of place, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Holmes finds freshly dug earth and judges it a decent lead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clue' here is a detective's evidence, not a crossword clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloodstain is the sort of physical evidence Sherlock Holmes would examine at a crime scene.

clue.text: Not any nuts for Land Rover?

blocks.note: no means not any
nuts means crazy

explanation.surface: A query about a missing supply of nuts for a Land Rover vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: Land Rover is a British make of off-road vehicle; read as two words it is someone who roams the land.
explanation.definitionFit: A nomad wanders from place to place over land, a rover in the literal sense.

clue.text: Golf club for Sir Henry, would you say?

indicators.note: what you say is heard rather than read, so the word is matched by its sound

blocks.note: first meaning: a club with a broad head, for long shots
second meaning: the conductor who founded the Proms concerts
the auxiliary verb is pronounced the same

explanation.surface: Asking which golf club Sir Henry would choose.
explanation.walkthrough: Three routes to one word: the golf club, the conductor Sir Henry Wood of the London Proms, and the sound of would.
explanation.definitionFit: Golfers call their long-distance clubs woods, and Henry Wood was the famous British conductor knighted in 1911.

clue.text: Orlando's on time, you say, needing no preparation

indicators.note: what you say is spoken, so a single letter that is pronounced like the word stands in

blocks.note: Orlando is the setter, so the setter's 'is' becomes I'M
prompt means punctual
the letter U is pronounced as you

explanation.surface: The setter turns up punctually, needing no rehearsal.
explanation.walkthrough: Orlando is this puzzle's setter, so 'Orlando's' means 'I am', I'M.
explanation.definitionFit: Something impromptu is done on the spur of the moment, without rehearsal or planning.

clue.text: Fancy sort of ticket

blocks.note: first meaning: to imagine or wish
second meaning: a ... ticket is an ideal pairing, as of election candidates

explanation.surface: A posh kind of admission ticket.
explanation.definitionFit: To dream is to fancy or imagine, and a dream ticket is a perfect combination of running mates.

clue.text: Nymph not serving alcohol, extremely awkward

indicators.note: extremely points to the extremes, the two ends of the next word

blocks.note: a dry bar or event serves no alcohol
the first and last letters of awkward

explanation.surface: A sprite at a teetotal party feels very uncomfortable.
explanation.definitionFit: A dryad is a tree nymph in Greek mythology.

clue.text: Damned business bigwig given assessment

blocks.note: short for executive
rated means assessed or valued

explanation.surface: A senior executive receives a damning performance review.
explanation.definitionFit: To execrate is to curse or denounce, so execrated is a past participle meaning cursed.
